name: Marco Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'm Marco, 27, apprentice lineworker with the electricity company in the town I grew up in. I'm engaged to Ania, who's a teaching assistant at the primary school, and we're getting married at St. Stanislaus church next June.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Then let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're the district crew, so we cover everything from the river out to the hill farms. Mostly it's fixing what storms and tractors break: a pole knocked over, a fuse blown on a transformer, a line down on a farm track. Dale, my foreman, makes me do the jobs the old way first, by hand, so I learn it properly. I like that. My dad did this job for 34 years, so half the farmers already know my face.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the new tech on the crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: As little as I can. The company gave us tablets for the job sheets and I let Dale fill mine in. I've never touched one of those AI chatbots and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I've been saying all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. I'd say it at the pub and to my dad, and probably at the men's breakfast after church. I'm not online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, which is what I want. My dad Jerzy climbed poles for this company for 34 years. I'd like to do the same, and in this picture I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at my apprenticeship and keep learning off Dale. I'd keep saving about 250 a month: the wedding first, then a deposit on a small house near my parents. That's my plan anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like things are as they should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's already on your mind about money, wedding aside or including it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, mainly. The hall, the band, Ania's dress, it adds up to more than I thought, maybe 9,000. Between us we've got about three months of bills saved after that, which is enough, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad say about all this AI talk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad says the company tried to replace meter readers with clever boxes years ago, and the boxes kept breaking. He thinks this is the same. I tend to believe him.

say: I'd say **I told you so** at the pub and after church.
AI is just another fad, like the **meter boxes** my dad saw break.
think: Nothing changes, which is **exactly what** I want.
I'd like to climb poles for **34 years**, like my dad.
do: Keep at the **apprenticeship** and keep learning off foreman Dale.
Save about **250 a month** for the wedding and then a house deposit.
feel: **Calm**, as if things are as they **should be**.
S0.quote: My dad Jerzy climbed poles for this company for 34 years. I'd like to do the same, and in this picture I can.
fieldNote: His model of a career is his **father's** 34 years with one company.
He avoids **tablets** and AI entirely and lets his foreman fill in forms.
The **wedding cost**, about 9,000, is his main money pressure.

steps.text: Keep learning district repairs the old way from foreman Dale
Save 250 a month for the wedding and a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's the office getting computers, mostly. Not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let the office have their computers. A pole still needs a man at the top of it, and I'm happy to be that man. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job's fine. The people who book jobs and answer the phones might be in trouble. And the tech companies get richer while everyone else adjusts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my work and keep saving. If the company made me use a new app, I'd use it, but I'd leave it to others to work out first. I'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm fine, but I don't like the direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone in your town feel this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ania's cousin Kasia works in the company's call centre in town. That's thirty people in one building. If half of those go, that's thirty families on our side of town feeling it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not us, but you also said you'd watch. Why watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what happened to the mill. Everyone said it was fine right up until the gates shut. I'd keep an eye out, that's all.

say: A **pole** still needs a man at the top of it.
Let the **office** have their computers; I'll stay on the lines.
think: **Tech companies** get richer while ordinary people adjust.
Call centre staff like **Kasia** are the ones in trouble.
do: Keep working the **district crew** as normal and keep saving.
Use any new **app** only after others have worked it out.
feel: **Uneasy** about the direction, though **his own** job feels fine.
S1.quote: Let the office have their computers. A pole still needs a man at the top of it, and I'm happy to be that man.
fieldNote: He blames **tech companies** rather than government for the shift.
The closed **mill** in his town is his reference for sudden loss.
He links job cuts to **families** on his side of town, a community view.

steps.text: Keep working the district crew and saving for the wedding
Leave the new job apps until others have tried them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And robots by 2031? That's the year I wanted our first child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built these machines should answer for it. I'd say it at church and at the pub. I wouldn't want handouts, I'd want my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancée Ania and I want kids by 2030. I can't start a family on a job that a robot takes the year after. And Ania's school job would be under the thinking AI too, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shrink the wedding to the church and the parish hall, no band, saving maybe 5,000. All of it goes in the bank. I'd ask Dad and my uncle Piotr, who's a builder, whether there's any work going if the line job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ania decide about the wedding and children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still marry, that's not in question. But kids would wait till we knew where the money was coming from. That would break Ania's heart, and mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. My parents, Ania's parents, and the parish. Father Tomasz always says the community looks after its own, and I'd be counting on it.

say: The people who built these machines should **answer for it**.
I'd want to **keep my job**, not take handouts from the government.
think: I can't start a **family** on a job robots take in 2031.
Ania's **school job** might be under threat too.
do: Cut the wedding to **church and parish hall**, saving about 5,000.
Put the saved **5,000** straight into the bank.
Ask **uncle Piotr** about building work if the line job goes.
feel: **Alarmed** and lying awake, which he says he never does.
S2.quote: My fiancée Ania and I want kids by 2030. I can't start a family on a job that a robot takes the year after.
fieldNote: The robot date of **2031** collides with his plan for a first child.
His safety net is **family and parish**, not government help.
No retraining at all: his only moves are **cutting and leaning** on relatives.
Rejects **handouts** while preparing to rely on community support.

steps.text: Cut the wedding back to church and parish hall
Bank the 5,000 saved from the smaller wedding
Put off having children until the money is clear
Ask uncle Piotr about building work as a fallback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots in 2034. I'd be 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the companies should train apprentices for whatever comes next, not just bin us. That's what a decent employer does. I'd say it to Dale and the union rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to get married, buy a house and find out it was the wrong house to buy. I'd be qualified and earning more, but with a mortgage and maybe a baby when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry as planned, but keep the house deposit in the bank another year or two and watch. I'd save 400 a month once I qualify. I'd wait and see what the company says before changing anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not the lying-awake kind, but there all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. I'd rent near my parents and see which way it goes by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn or try in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I don't trust the new stuff. If Dale or my dad said it was worth learning, I might.

say: Companies should **train apprentices** for what comes next.
A **decent employer** doesn't just bin its people when new machines arrive.
think: I'd have a **mortgage** and maybe a baby when the robots arrive.
Five years could be just enough to **buy the wrong house**.
do: Marry as planned but hold the **house deposit** a year or two.
Wait for the **company's plan** before changing anything else.
feel: **Anxious**, a steady worry rather than sleepless nights.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to get married, buy a house and find out it was the wrong house to buy.
fieldNote: His fear is about **timing**: big commitments landing just before robots.
Prefers **employer training** to state help, in line with his traditional view.
Would only learn new tech if **Dale or his dad** vouched for it.

steps.text: Hold the house deposit and rent near his parents until 2030
Wait for the company's robot plan before changing trades

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 39 when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for the company to look after its own. I'd expect them to, and I'd say so. I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'd have kids in school and a mortgage, and I still can't picture myself doing anything but this. That's the worry, not the robots exactly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding, the house and children as planned. I'd keep saving and wait to see what the company offers around 2034. I wouldn't jump trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quieter. It's a long way off, but I'd be the one with the most to lose by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Why still worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is enough time for me to get comfortable and stop paying attention. My dad never had to change, and I'm built the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade that needs a person's hands and a person's judgement. Whatever that is by then. I wouldn't know.

say: Ten years is enough for the company to **look after** its own.
I'd expect that and **say so**, without shouting.
think: By then I'd have **kids and a mortgage**.
I can't picture myself doing **anything else**, and that's the worry.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding, house and children** as planned.
Keep saving and **wait** for the company's offer around 2034.
feel: **Anxious** but quieter, knowing he'd have **most to lose** later.
S4.quote: In ten years I'd have kids in school and a mortgage, and I still can't picture myself doing anything but this.
fieldNote: More time means **more commitments** stacked up before robots, not more preparation.
He knows he will **stop paying attention**, like his father never had to.
His **resistance** to change is the thread through all five pictures.

steps.text: Go ahead with the wedding, house and children as planned
Keep working the district crew and saving each month
Wait for the company's offer around 2034 before switching

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It hits right when Ania and I want to start a family. Every family on our street had someone at the power company or the mill. The mill's gone, and I don't want the power company going the same way. What would help is the company keeping its apprentices and training us for whatever comes next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the town. When one big employer goes, it's not one job, it's the bakery, the church collection, the football club. Everybody feels it.

headlineQuote: Every family on our street had someone at the power company or the mill. The mill's gone, and I don't want the power company going the same way.
portrait: Marco is a 27-year-old **apprentice** lineworker in his home town, engaged to Ania, a teaching assistant.
His father worked **34 years** for the same company, and that's the career Marco wants.
He never uses **AI** and lets his foreman fill in his tablet forms.
He is **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 because robots would arrive just as he wants children.
He relies on **family and parish** rather than retraining or government help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which lands as he and Ania plan to start a family.
whatWouldHelp: The company **keeping apprentices** and training them for what comes next.
